conceptTag: Write a recommendation to your boss
readerTitle: How to write a recommendation your boss can say yes to
caseNote: 가상 사례 (비스트로의 월요일 점심 영업, 소프트웨어 출시 연기) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 추천 메일은 정보 정리가 아니라 상사가 바로 결정할 수 있게 만드는 글이다. 답을 먼저 쓰고, 그 답의 대가를 스스로 밝힌다.
misconception: 배경부터 차근차근 설명해야 설득력이 생기고, 단점은 숨겨야 승인받기 쉽다.

sources.text: 모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 비스트로 수치는 가상입니다. 월요일 점심 매출 약 $400, 인건비·준비비 약 $550, 주당 약 $150 손실, 9시간 재배치. 계산을 다시 확인하세요.
소프트웨어 사례의 '테스트 사용자 5명 중 1명이 가입을 끝내지 못함'은 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 통계처럼 읽히지 않도록 카드에 illustrative 표시를 했습니다.

cards.title: "So what do you want me to do?"
body: Maya, assistant manager at a small bistro, spent an evening writing to the owner. Three careful paragraphs on slow Monday lunches, staff hours and busy weekends.
The owner read it on her phone between deliveries and replied with one line: *"So what do you want me to do?"*
Maya had a clear recommendation. She just never wrote it down where anyone would find it.

image.label: Restaurant owner frowning at a long message on her phone
image.brief: 주방 뒷문 앞에서 식재료 상자를 든 채 휴대폰을 보는 식당 주인. 화면에는 긴 문단이 빽빽하고, 말풍선으로 "So what do you want me to do?"만 짧게 표시. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: How should Maya's rewrite begin?
body: Maya wants to close Monday lunch and move those staff hours to Friday and Saturday dinner, when the bistro turns guests away.
Which opening gives her the best chance of a quick, clear answer?

options.text: "Over the past two months I've been tracking our Monday lunch numbers…"
options.feedback: It shows effort, but the owner has to read to the end to learn what's being asked. That's the problem *lead with the answer* solves.

options.text: "I recommend we close Monday lunch and move those hours to weekend dinners. Can we decide by Friday?"
options.feedback: **Lead with the answer:** the owner knows the ask and the deadline in one sentence. The reasons that follow now read as support, not suspense.

options.text: "Here are three options for Monday lunch. Which do you prefer?"
options.feedback: Options are useful, but this hands the thinking back to a busy owner. Pick one, then show the others as what you considered.

cards.title: Four lines the owner can read in a minute.
body: Same facts as before, in a new order. The answer comes first; everything after it earns its place by supporting or testing that answer.

breakdown.label: The answer
breakdown.detail: Close Monday lunch, add 9 staff hours to weekend dinners

breakdown.label: Why
breakdown.detail: Monday lunch brings in about $400 and costs about $550 to run

breakdown.label: What it costs us
breakdown.detail: A few Monday regulars may stop coming

breakdown.label: The ask
breakdown.detail: Decide by Friday so the new rota starts next month

cards.softwareNote: The same four lines work for a pricing change or a hiring request. Teams that write in tools like chat or email get skimmed too, so the first line does most of the work.

cards.title: What should Maya say about the downside?
body: A handful of regulars love the quiet Monday lunch. Closing it could annoy them. How should line 3 handle this?

options.text: Leave it out. It only gives the owner a reason to say no
options.feedback: The owner knows those regulars by name and will think of them anyway. If you skipped it, she'll wonder what else you skipped.

options.text: Name it, compare it with the gain, and say how to soften it
options.feedback: **Presenting trade-offs:** you show what you give up, why the gain is bigger, and a plan to limit the loss, such as a regulars' discount on another weekday.

options.text: List every risk she can think of, to look thorough
options.feedback: Honest, but ten small risks bury the one that matters. Name the main cost clearly and drop the noise.

cards.title: Naming the cost builds trust.
body: A boss reading a recommendation is checking two things: is this a good idea, and can I trust this person's judgment?
When you raise the downside yourself, you answer both. You show you saw the cost, weighed it, and still think the gain is bigger. That is **the trade-off** in plain view.
A recommendation with no visible cost looks like a sales pitch. One with an honest cost looks like a decision already half made.

image.label: A balance scale with gain on one side and cost on the other
image.brief: 단순한 저울 일러스트. 무거운 쪽에 "Busier weekends", 가벼운 쪽에 "Some Monday regulars". 옆에 작은 메모지 "Plan: regulars' discount". 따뜻한 색감.

cards.title: Leading with the answer isn't faking certainty.
body: If you're not sure, say so in the first line: *"I lean toward closing Monday lunch, but want to test it for four weeks first."* That's still an answer.
Some bosses also need one line of context before the ask, especially if the topic is new to them. Add that one line, not three paragraphs.
And a trade-off should be real. Inventing a tiny cost to look balanced fools no one for long.

cards.title: Now it's a software launch.
body: You lead a product team. Launch is set for the 6th, timed with a conference demo. In testing, about 1 in 5 new users couldn't finish signing up.
You want to delay two weeks. Which first message to your CEO is strongest?

options.text: "I recommend moving launch to the 20th. We lose the conference demo, but we fix a sign-up bug that blocked 1 in 5 test users."
options.feedback: Both ideas at work: the answer leads, and the trade-off sits right beside it. The CEO can judge the demo against lost sign-ups in one read.

options.text: "Here's a full timeline of the bugs we found in testing."
options.feedback: Useful detail for later, but the CEO has to guess what you want. Lead with the answer, then attach the timeline.

options.text: "Should we delay launch? There are pros and cons."
options.feedback: It flags the issue, but without your recommendation or the specific cost. Your CEO asked you because you know the trade-off best.

cards.softwareNote: In software, the cost of a delay is often a missed moment, like a demo or a marketing push. Name that moment, not just "two weeks."

cards.title: Make it easy to say yes, and safe to say no.
body: A good recommendation lets your boss decide in one read, with the real cost already on the table.
**Try it today:** take a request you're about to send. Move your recommendation to the first line, and add one sentence on what it costs.
list: **Lead with the answer:** the ask and the deadline come first
**Presenting trade-offs:** name the cost, compare it with the gain, show how to soften it
